title: Toilet Flange Height Solutions: Wax Seal, Shims, and a New Long-Bolt Kit (Ask This Old House)
summary: This Old House’s Ask This Old House episode explains the critical seal beneath a toilet between the toilet flange and the sewer line, detailing typical components, failure modes, and practical DIY solutions for height or wobble issues. The segment covers standard configurations (closet flange, wax seal, bolts), how a floor with rot or raised grades affects sealing, and common strategies to adjust height (flange shims, plywood underlayment). It then introduces an advanced flange kit with longer bolts and integrated wax-seal hardware designed to accommodate significant up- or down- building, including a low-profile mounting method with captive fasteners and a “shock-absorber” style mechanism to preserve a positive seal during installation. The discussion highlights trade-offs, such as the potential need for a plumber for pipe modification versus DIY shim-and-kit approaches, and ends with practical tips on trimming bolts and finishing hardware.

title: Toilet Tank Evolution: High-Tank (1880s) to Modern Flush Valve
summary: This Old House host walks through the anatomy of a late-19th-century high-tank toilet and contrasts it with a contemporary tank, illustrating how different components functioned, why older systems were prone to failure, and how modern designs achieve reliable flushing with far less water. The discussion identifies four legacy parts (tank lever, flush valve, fill valve, and copper-walled tank with a copper tank ball float) and traces the transition to a modern flush valve with a flapper, a two-shank overflow, an adjustable fill valve, and a refill tube. The narrative explains the flow path during flush, the role of the siphon jet, and how bowl refill maintains proper water level. It also covers practical maintenance by highlighting two key adjustments—tank lever travel and float level—to ensure a one-flush, water-saving operation, including recommended target water level (about three-quarters of an inch below the overflow).

title: Repair Toilet Tank Components: Flapper Replacement, Chain Adjustment, and Fill-Valve Settings
summary: This This Old House segment explains how a standard toilet tank works by distinguishing the flush valve (including the flapper) from the fill valve, and then demonstrates practical repair steps to stop common leaks. The host emphasizes that leaks inside the tank waste water, and walks through identifying a worn flapper, replacing it, and adjusting the chain so the tank lever operates correctly. The video also covers setting the fill-valve height so the tank stops filling about one inch below the overflow, discusses the difference between old brass float rods and modern built-in floats, and highlights safety considerations of the overflow tube. Throughout, the emphasis is on turning off the water before work, testing after each adjustment, and avoiding over-tightening to prevent recurrent leaks.

title: Converting a Toilet to Dual-Flush: Retrofit, Valve Installation, and Bowl Refilling
summary: This Old House walks a homeowner through converting an existing 3.5 gallons-per-flush toilet into a dual-flush model using a retrofit valve and a two-button actuator. The video covers removing the old tank lever, installing a dual-flush valve with a blue gasket, attaching a two-button actuator (one for liquids, one for solids), and reconfiguring the fill valve to ensure the bowl refills adequately after a reduced liquid flush. The host demonstrates turning off the water, draining the tank, wiring and securing components, and then testing a liquid flush that uses significantly less water while preserving a full flush for solids. A noted tradeoff is that the bowl needs adequate refill water, prompting a later adjustment with an adjustable fill valve and refill tube to restore proper bowl performance. The segment ends with a recap of how to use the top (liquids) and bottom (solids) buttons and the expected water savings.

summary: This This Old House video presents a retrofit approach to turn a standard toilet into a graywater-capable unit by adding an integrated hand-wash sink above the tank. A spacer is introduced to accommodate different tank lengths. The clip concludes with the claim that the kit can be installed on standard toilets to provide a dedicated hand-washing sink while maintaining the standard bowl refill cycle. title: How a Plumbing Trap Can Lose Water: Traps, Vents, and Common Causes
summary: This Old House explains how a washing machine drain can pull water out of a toilet trap when a vent is absent or clogged, by using a mock-up to illustrate traps and water seals. The video defines key plumbing elements—P-traps, toilet traps, and vent pipes—and demonstrates how a vent allows air into the drainage system to prevent negative pressure and gurgling. It contrasts unvented versus vented drain conditions, discusses where vents should connect, and covers several mechanisms that can cause trap seals to fail, including oscillation from wind, siphonage with S-traps, capillary action, evaporation, and momentum. The host offers practical notes on checking vents, considering mechanical vent options, and refilling traps if sewer gas smells occur.

title: Toilet Tank Rebuild: Replacing Fill and Flush Valves and Fine-Tuning Float
summary: This Old House provides a step-by-step tank-rebuild demonstration focused on diagnosing and correcting leaks in a toilet tank. The host explains the core components—the flapper/flush valve, the fill valve, the float, and the overflow tube—and how flushing and refilling work. Historical notes compare brass and copper components to modern plastic equivalents, noting that floats became integral to the valve in contemporary designs. The video then covers diagnosing a running toilet (faulty flapper seating, worn or misadjusted fill valve, or overflow-driven overfill), draining the tank, and removing the old valves. A universal repair kit is installed to replace both valves, seal the tank-to-bowl with a spud gasket, and reassemble. Final steps include positioning the refill tube, adjusting the float height, and ensuring the water level sits about one inch below the overflow to prevent leaks. The host also cautions against overtightening and provides a rough price point (~$20) for the kit.

title: Repairing a Rotted Cast-Iron Toilet Flange with a Retrofit Gasket and Spacer System
summary: This Old House’s tutorial walks through diagnosing a leak tied to a failed wax seal and a rotted cast-iron closet flange after a bathroom remodel. A remodel revealed the old cast-iron flange was missing or severely degraded, prompting a retrofit approach: replace with a gasket-style flange adapter designed for cast-iron pipe, using spacers to set the correct height, and switching from a traditional wax seal to a flexible gasket.
